title: Eight spokes, one wheel
hookLine: the eight factors in three trainings: wisdom, conduct, meditation (MN 44)
last: THE TRUTHS — FOUR TRUTHS, ONE PATH.

cards: The commentaries tell the backstory. A merchant named Visakha comes home from hearing the Buddha teach, changed for good, and his wife, Dhammadinna, notices.

Soon she goes forth as a nun, practices hard, and, tradition says, becomes fully awakened. One day Visakha visits her and, instead of small talk, asks her question after question about the teaching. She answers every one.
When he reports the conversation to the Buddha, the Buddha says he would have answered exactly the same way.

teach.b: The conversation is in the Middle-Length Discourses, number forty-four.
One of Visakha's questions is about how the path fits together: are the three trainings included in the noble eightfold path, or is the path included in the three trainings?
Dhammadinna answers that the eight are sorted into the three.

Right speech, right action and right livelihood belong to conduct, sila: how you live with others. Right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration belong to meditation, samadhi: how you train the mind.
Right view and right intention belong to wisdom, panna: how you see, and what you aim for. Eight factors, three trainings. Now the wheel.
The dharma wheel with eight spokes is a later symbol, carved and painted all over Asia, on temple gates and flags. But it fits her answer. A wheel with a missing spoke still turns, badly.
A wheel with all eight runs true. And no spoke comes first: they all meet at the hub and touch the rim at once.

The path's own list starts with right view, so some teachers say wisdom comes first: you need a view to start walking. Dhammadinna names conduct first, so others say a calm, honest life is the ground for everything else.
Both orders are in the texts.

teach.h: THE TRAININGS LEAN ON EACH OTHER.
teach.b: What they agree on is that the three trainings lean on each other, like the spokes.
Over the next weeks, we'll take each spoke on its own, starting tomorrow with right view. And remember who drew this map: a nun, whose answers the Buddha said he would have given himself.

how: Buddhist teachers commonly teach the eightfold path through the three trainings of conduct, meditation and wisdom, and the eight-spoked dharma wheel appears on temples, flags and books across Asia.

o: the eight path factors, turning as one
eight rules for a nun's daily life
eight monks who spread the teaching

games.q: match each factor to its training.
p: the nun who sorted the eight

s: the eight-spoked wheel appears in the first sermon
it's a later symbol; the sermon speaks of setting the wheel rolling but doesn't count spokes.
the Buddha said he would have answered Visakha just as Dhammadinna did
he approved her answers in MN 44.
right effort belongs to the training in wisdom
Dhammadinna puts effort, mindfulness and concentration under meditation.

games.q: you're Visakha. you've just heard Dhammadinna's answers and reported them to the Buddha. what does he say?
o: she got some of it wrong.
he would have answered the same way.
a nun shouldn't teach a layman.
games.why: the Buddha says Dhammadinna is wise, and that he would have explained it exactly as she did.

practice: Picture three bowls in front of you: conduct, meditation, wisdom.
Breathe, and drop each factor into its bowl: speech, action and livelihood into conduct; effort, mindfulness and concentration into meditation; view and intention into wisdom.
Then picture the three bowls set around a single wheel, and let the wheel turn slowly with your breath.

wordCard.voice: Eight spokes. The eight factors of the path, sorted by the nun Dhammadinna into three trainings: conduct, meditation and wisdom, all turning together.

orig.note: Pali sikkhā: training; the three trainings are conduct (sīla), meditation (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā).

carryVoice: Your line: all meet at the hub. Each training leans on the other two. That's day three hundred fifty-three.
